💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach. He loves speaking at conferences like Smashing Conf and is a founding member of the Adobe Design … More about Andy ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way. Not always in those exact words, obviously. It usually comes out as something more reasonable: we didn’t get enough engineering time, product had already decided the solution, the roadmap was too packed, leadership only cared about this quarter’s numbers, research got cut, the experiment was never run properly, the design debt was known about, but nobody wanted to spend a sprint fixing it.

Much of this is true. Most designers have worked inside that awkward middle space between product and engineering. Product frames the problem, or at least thinks it does. Engineering decides what is feasible, or at least what is affordable. Design is expected to make the thing clearer, simpler, more coherent, more usable, and occasionally more desirable, while also being careful not to disrupt the strategy too much.

That position has always been uncomfortable.

They can spot the broken onboarding flow, the confusing upgrade path, the empty state that makes consumers feel stupid, the feature that looks reasonable in a product review but makes no sense in real use. Seeing the problem is one thing. Getting it fixed is another.

According to recent reports, so design often becomes an argument. You make the case. You annotate the flow. You bring the research clip. You point to the support tickets. You show the Figma prototype. You explain why the “small edge case” is actually the first-run experience for half your new customers. Then everyone nods, agrees it matters, and moves on to whatever had already made it onto the roadmap.

According to recent reports, this is one reason AI is more interesting for design than the usual “will it replace designers?” debate suggests. The real change is not that designers can make more screens. Nobody needs more screens. The interesting change is that designers may need less permission.

A good designer can now move from “we should fix this” to “I fixed this, and pushed it live.” They can prototype the alternative onboarding flow, write and test clearer product copy, build a rough working version of the interaction, clean up small pieces of design debt without waiting three months for a roadmap slot, and make the better thing visible enough that it becomes harder to ignore.

Sources indicate that that changes the politics of the work. Design has often relied on persuasion because designers lacked direct means of production. AI weakens that dependency. Not everywhere, and not for everything. Complex products still have architecture, infrastructure, data models, permissions, security, compliance, legacy systems, and all the other unglamorous reasons software is hard. But the boundary is moving.

Industry observers note that in this version of the future, designers become less permission-dependent: less reliant on product to bless the problem, less reliant on engineering to make every small improvement real, less trapped in the role of internal critic, taste-provider, or Figma operator. More able to make, test, repair, and ship.

Recent findings suggest that the best designers start to look less like traditional product designers and more like hybrid product leaders. They still care about interaction, hierarchy, language, flow, brand and craft, but they also understand the commercial shape of the problem. They can make trade-offs. They can prototype in code, or close enough to code. They can use AI to explore options quickly, then use judgment to throw most of them away. They can sit with a founder or PM and move from a vague product concern to something tangible by the end of the day.

Recent findings suggest that there may be fewer of these people, but they will be harder to ignore. The current design-org model was partly built around scarcity: scarce engineering time, slow production, expensive prototypes, handoffs between specialists, heavy coordination across teams. If AI reduces some of that scarcity, it probably reduces the need for some of the roles that grew around it. The optimistic case is not that every designer keeps their job and gets a productivity boost. That feels like wishful thinking. The more believable version is that the total number of designers goes down, but the designers who remain have more direct influence over the product.

According to recent reports, that is not a bad outcome for the strongest designers. It may even be the thing many of them have wanted for years.

Autonomy has teeth. If AI gives designers more room to act, it also removes some of the cover. The same constraints that held good designers back have also protected weaker ones from being tested too directly.

Sources indicate that for years, it has been easy to say: I had a better idea, but we never got the engineering time. Sometimes that was exactly what happened. Sometimes the better idea was never really more than a critique. It had not been made concrete. It had not been tested. It had not dealt with the awkward trade-offs. It sounded strong because it lived safely in opposition to the shipped thing.

Sources indicate that if you can prototype the recommendation, the recommendation has to get better. If you can make the alternative flow, the flow has to survive contact with details. If you can test the product copy, you have to care what happens when users read it. If you can fix the small piece of design debt, you have to decide whether it was really worth fixing.

Sources indicate that some designers are not as strategic as they think they are. They have learned the language of strategy without the discomfort of owning outcomes. They can talk about user needs, business goals, systems thinking, and product quality, but struggle when asked to make a call. They want influence, but not the exposure that comes with it.

Industry observers note that the profession has spent a long time arguing that design deserves more power. Fine. But more power means fewer excuses. It means the work is judged less by the elegance of the argument and more by the quality of the thing you made, tested, or changed. That is a better standard, but it will not be kind to everyone.

Sources indicate that there is a second bear case, and it is probably the one large design teams should worry about most. Product and engineering already have more institutional power than design in most companies. They own the roadmap, the technical architecture, the sprint machinery, the metrics, and usually the language leadership understands. Design often has to translate its concerns into someone else’s terms before they count.

It has been revealed that AI may not rebalance that power. It may hand product and engineering enough design capability to make design easier to bypass. A PM who can generate a decent flow, decent copy, and a decent prototype may not feel the same need to involve design early. An engineer who can use AI to produce a reasonable interface may decide the design system covers enough of the decision-making. A founder who can get to a polished demo in an afternoon may confuse polish with product thinking.

The problem is not that these people will suddenly become great designers. The problem is that many companies do not know the difference between great design and plausible design. Plausible design is dangerous. It looks coherent in a product review. It uses the right components. The spacing is fine. The copy is not embarrassing. The flow mostly works. Nobody in the meeting feels strongly enough to object. So it ships.

If a company already thinks design is mostly screens, prototypes, and polish, AI gives it a cheaper way to get those things.

In that world, design does not gain more agency. It gets narrowed. The remaining designers manage the design system, police component usage, review flows that have already been decided, tidy the interface, maintain brand consistency, and get pulled into high-stakes launches, executive demos, and the occasional messy cross-platform problem. Useful work, but a smaller surface area. Less shaping the product, more maintaining the furniture.

According to recent reports, this is why the “AI will automate the boring 20%” argument feels too comforting. In some companies, perhaps that is what happens. But in large tech organisations, where design teams grew around coordination, production and process, the cut could be much deeper. Not 20%. Maybe 50%. Maybe more. Especially in places where leadership never really understood why the design team had grown so large in the first place.

The painful part is that both futures can be true at the same time. AI can make the best designers more capable and many average designers less necessary. It can give design more agency while reducing design headcount. It can help a small number of designers move closer to product leadership while pushing others into governance and clean-up work. It can free designers from waiting for permission, then reveal that some were more comfortable waiting than acting.

According to recent reports, the designers who do well will not be the ones who merely use AI to produce more options. Options are cheap now. They will be the ones who know which option is worth pursuing, why it matters, how to test it, what to cut, where the product is lying to itself, and when “good enough” is quietly damaging the business.

They will have taste, but taste will not be enough. They will need product judgment, technical curiosity, commercial awareness and the nerve to make decisions before every variable is settled. They will need to be comfortable moving between a customer conversation, a prototype, a pricing concern, a brand question, and a messy implementation detail without insisting that all of those belong to someone else.

I’m not completely sure where we end up. I hope it is closer to the bull case: fewer permission structures, more making, more agency, better designers finally able to show what they can do without being held back by the machinery around them.

I fear it may be closer to the bear case: product and engineering absorb much of the work, companies decide plausible design is good enough, and design loses status, headcount, and strategic ground.

In a recent development, in reality, it will probably be some uncomfortable mix of the two. Some designers will use AI to gain more agency. Some companies will use it to need fewer designers. Some teams will produce better work because the distance between judgment and execution gets shorter. Others will ship more plausible mediocrity because nobody in the room can tell the difference.

Sources indicate that for years, designers have said they could create more value if they were less constrained by the organisation around them. AI is about to test that claim. Some will finally get to prove it. Some will find out the constraints were doing them a favour.

Industry observers note that picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

It has been revealed that the primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Sources indicate that another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

  • According to recent reports, vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali has formed a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

According to recent reports, vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative.

According to recent reports, “It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali claims. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”.

In a recent development, informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali notes. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”.

As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”.

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

It has been revealed that shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

Sources indicate that A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?

My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again. It does its job, the tests pass, and we move on. But the web platform keeps moving too, and a surprising number of the libraries sitting in your package.json today are now built into the browser.

Recent findings suggest that in a typical mid-sized JavaScript app, you can often find somewhere between 60KB and 90KB (minified and gzipped) of dependencies that the platform can now handle on its own. Date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays: these were all real gaps a few years ago. A lot of them aren’t gaps anymore.

Industry observers note that the reason those libraries stick around isn’t laziness. It’s that most teams don’t re-audit their dependencies on a Baseline cadence, or are simply not aware of how fast browsers are shipping these days. You check npm audit for security, but is this library still doing something the browser can’t? is a question that rarely gets asked. So the libraries stay.

According to recent reports, in this article, we’ll run that audit together. Instead of going through dependencies one by one, we’ll work in clusters, because the wins tend to come in groups. We’ll do the bundle math, build a small decision framework you can reuse, and stay honest about the cases where the platform still falls short. By the end, you’ll have a repeatable process you can run on your own package.json.

According to recent reports, before we start deleting things, let’s quickly recap what Baseline is. Feel free to skip this section if you’re already familiar.

Baseline is a project from the WebDX Community Group that tells you, in plain terms, how safe a web feature is to use across the major browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari). A feature can be in one of three states:.

That 30-month gap between “Newly” and “Widely” matters a lot for this audit. A feature that’s Widely available is something you can usually drop a library for today. A feature that’s only Newly available is something you can drop a library for if you check your audience first, or if you’re comfortable with a small feature check. We’ll treat those two cases differently throughout.

Recent findings suggest that you can look any feature up on webstatus.dev, on MDN (every reference page reveals a Baseline badge near the top), or programmatically with the web-features npm package. We’ll use all three later when we run the audit on a real project.

According to recent reports, it’s tempting to read “the browser does this now” and start ripping libraries out. Let’s not do that. A swap that looks free on paper can quietly break things for a chunk of your users, or cost you a feature you were relying on without realizing it.

So before dropping any library, ask three questions. We’ll reuse these in every cluster below.

1. Is the replacement Baseline-safe for my audience?

Sources indicate that not “is it Baseline” in the abstract, but “is it safe for the people who actually use my app.” If the native feature is Widely available, this is usually a yes. If it’s only Newly available, check your analytics or your browserslist config and see what share of your users would miss out. A B2B dashboard where everyone’s on the latest browser is a very different situation from a public-facing site with a long tail of old Android devices.

According to recent reports, 2. What does the swap actually cost?

In a recent development, dropping a library isn’t always free. Sometimes the native feature isn’t supported widely enough yet, so you’d reach for a polyfill. If that polyfill is heavier than the library you’re removing, you’ve made your bundle bigger, unless you load it conditionally. We’ll see exactly this with Temporal later.

Industry observers note that 3. Does the platform feature cover my real use case?

Industry observers note that libraries often do more than the platform feature they resemble. axios isn’t just fetch with automatic JSON parsing; it has interceptors, request cancellation, and retries. If you’re using those, a straight swap to fetch will leave you reimplementing them. Check what you actually use before assuming it’s a drop-in replacement.

In a recent development, keep these three in mind. Every cluster below is really just these questions applied to a different corner of your dependencies.

This is the cluster where you’ll usually find the most KBs sitting on top of features that are already Widely available. The browser ships a whole family of formatting tools under the Intl namespace, and a lot of small, popular libraries became unnecessary.

Here are the usual suspects and what replaces them:.

Let’s walk through some of them.

Sources indicate that timeago.js exists to turn a timestamp into “3 hours ago”. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does the same thing, and it’s Baseline Widely available.

The numeric: "auto" option is the nice touch here: it gives you “yesterday” instead of “1 day ago” where the language has a word for it. You pass a number and a unit, and you get a localized string back.

You may be wondering about the one thing timeago.js does that this snippet doesn’t: it picks the unit for you. Given a date, timeago.js decides whether to say “seconds” or “days.” Intl.RelativeTimeFormat expects you to do that part. It’s a few lines of arithmetic (work out the difference, find the largest unit that fits), and once you’ve written that helper, you don’t need the library anymore.

Intl.NumberFormat covers most of what number-formatting libraries do: thousands separators, currency, percentages, and compact notation.

And Intl.ListFormat, Widely available, handles the “join an array into a sentence” problem, including the Oxford comma, which is the kind of thing people write fiddly helper functions for:.

In a recent development, humanize-duration turns a number of milliseconds into “1 hour, 30 minutes”. The platform equivalent is Intl.DurationFormat:.

One thing to keep in mind is that Intl.DurationFormat is Baseline Newly available at the time of writing, not Widely available. It landed in all the major engines in March 2025, and it’s on track to become Widely available in 2027. So this one fails question 1 for broad-audience apps unless you check your traffic first or add a fallback. For an internal tool on modern browsers, it’s fine today. For a public site with old devices, give it another year or guard it with a feature check.

It has been revealed that if your app uses the full set (humanize-duration, timeago.js, pluralize, numeral), that’s roughly 14 KB gzipped of dependencies, most of it replaceable right now with Widely available APIs. The internationalization cluster is usually the easiest win in the whole audit.

This cluster is more nuanced, so it’s a good one to slow down on.

The browser HTTP libraries people reach for are axios (17 KB gz) and superagent (19 KB gz). For most requests, fetch plus AbortController covers what you need, and both are Widely available.

The one extra line (res.json()) is fetch being explicit where axios was implicit. That’s the pattern across this whole cluster: fetch does less for you by default, and you decide whether you want the things it leaves out.

In a recent development, axios has a timeout option. fetch has AbortSignal.timeout():.

This is where question 3 does most of the work, so let’s be specific about the gaps:.

I personally heavily rely on interceptors in my interactive online courses, such as Learn JavaScript, and I have solved that for years using a custom class on top of fetch. I’ve shipped this to millions of customers and have seen lots of success with it.

None of these are hard to rebuild, and most apps only use one or two of them. But this is exactly the kind of cluster where you shouldn’t do a blind find-and-replace. Look at how you actually use your HTTP client first. If it’s plain GETs and POSTs, dropping axios for a thin fetch wrapper saves you about 17 KB gzipped.

This cluster has some of the most satisfying swaps, because the platform features don’t just match the libraries, they’re often more accessible than what teams ship by hand.

Sources indicate that the libraries here are modal dialogs (something like a11y-dialog, 1.8 KB gz), tooltip and popover libraries (tippy.js, 14 KB gz, which bundles Popper for positioning), focus-trap (6.6 KB gz), and body-scroll-lock (1.3 KB gz). They get replaced by three platform features: the element, the Popover API, and CSS anchor positioning.

According to recent reports, A huge amount of modal-related code exists to solve accessibility problems: trapping focus inside the modal, closing on Escape, restoring focus to the previous element when the dialog is closed, and rendering above everything else. The element, Widely available, does all of that for you.

Industry observers note that calling showModal() does the work that focus-trap was installed for: focus moves into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert so you can’t tab out of it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The dialog renders in the browser’s Top layer, so you don’t fight z-index. You also get a ::backdrop pseudo-element to style the overlay.

Sources indicate that that single element can replace your modal library and focus-trap. The one piece it doesn’t handle on its own is locking the background from scrolling, which is what body-scroll-lock was for. That’s now one line of CSS:.

If you’re wondering why we’re using dialog:modal instead of dialog[open], it’s because the open attribute is set as soon as you call show(), but the dialog isn’t actually modal so you don’t want to lock scrolling yet. The :modal pseudo-class is only true when the dialog is actually modal, which is the case when you call showModal().

So three libraries collapse into one element and one CSS rule.

For things that aren’t full modals (dropdown menus, tooltips, the small floating panels that tippy.js handles), the Popover API gives you light-dismiss behavior, top-layer rendering, and Escape-to-close with no JavaScript at all:.

According to recent reports, clicking the button toggles the popover. Clicking outside it closes it. It’s Baseline Newly available (since January 2025).

Recent findings suggest that the other half of what a tooltip library does is positioning: keeping the floating element pinned to its trigger and flipping it when it would overflow the viewport. That’s what Popper (bundled inside tippy.js) handles, and it’s now a CSS feature called anchor positioning. Here it pins the same #menu popover directly under its trigger button:.

Anchor positioning is the newest feature in this article. It became Baseline Newly available in January 2026, when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome had it since version 125, and Safari since version 26). Because it’s this fresh, it’s squarely a question-1 feature: great for modern audiences, but check your traffic, and note that some of the more advanced parts (like position-try fallbacks) have uneven support across versions. Keep a sensible fallback for older browsers.

Between , the Popover API, and anchor positioning, the UI primitives cluster (tooltip library, modal library, focus-trap, body-scroll-lock) adds up to roughly 24 KB gzipped, and you come out the other side with better accessibility defaults than most hand-rolled solutions.

Recent findings suggest that lodash is rarely imported whole anymore, but its individual functions show up everywhere, either as the full lodash package (25 KB gz) or as standalone installs like lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby. Several of the most common ones now have direct platform equivalents.

lodash.groupby reorganizes an array into an object keyed by some property. Object.groupBy does exactly that:.

It has been revealed that there’s also Map.groupBy for when you want a Map instead of a plain object (handy if your keys aren’t strings). Both are Baseline Newly available, since March 2024, and on track to become Widely available in late 2026.

lodash.clonedeep makes a deep copy of an object. structuredClone is the platform version, and it’s Widely available:.

structuredClone handles the tricky cases that trip up JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)): it clones Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and circular references correctly. The limit to know about (question 3 again) is that it can’t clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances; it throws on functions and drops the prototype on class instances. For plain data, which is what most people deep-clone, it’s a clean replacement.

According to recent reports, if you’ve ever pulled in a Lodash helper for union, intersection, or difference, the Set object now has these built in. They’re Baseline Newly available, since June 2024:.

The full set of methods is union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom.

Not all of Lodash has moved into the platform. debounce and throttle still have no native equivalent, and they’re genuinely useful, so cherry-picking lodash.debounce is reasonable. The point of this cluster isn’t “delete Lodash,” it’s “stop shipping the parts the browser already has.” Dropping lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby alone is about 8 KB gzipped, and if you were importing the full lodash for a handful of functions, replacing the platform-covered ones can let you drop it entirely.

Every cluster so far has ended in “go ahead, drop it.” This one is the opposite, and that’s why it’s worth including: it shows the framework telling you to wait.

Temporal is the long-awaited replacement for JavaScript’s Date, and it’s a genuinely better API: immutable objects, sane time zone handling, and no more month indexes starting at zero. It reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of the ES2026 specification. Firefox shipped it in version 139 (in 2025), and Chrome shipped it in version 144 (January 2026). Safari hasn’t shipped it in a stable release yet; it’s in Safari Technology Preview, with stable support expected later in 2026.

If Temporal is news to you, check out the Temporal Cheatsheet for a quick overview of the API and a comparison to Date.

However, Temporal is not Baseline. It’s still in limited availability, because Safari users don’t have it. To use it across all browsers today, you need a polyfill, and this is where the math turns against you.

Sources indicate that the official @js-temporal/polyfill is about 44 KB gzipped. There’s a smaller polyfill that internally does not depend on BigInt and it weighs 19 KB gzipped. A lightweight date library like dayjs is about 3 KB gzipped. So if you swap dayjs for Temporal plus its polyfill right now, you’re not saving 3 KB, you’re adding roughly 41 KB to your bundle, unless you are able to load the polyfill conditionally.

In a recent development, the verdict is generally clear: keep dayjs (or date-fns) for now. The moment to revisit is when Safari ships Temporal in a stable release and it reaches Baseline. At that point you can use Temporal natively and conditionally load the polyfill for users on older browsers. This is a feature to write down and check again in a few months, not one to act on today.

The clusters above are a starting map, but your dependencies are your own. Here’s a repeatable process you can run this quarter.

Start by listing what actually ships to customers:.

In a recent development, for a quick per-package number, Bundlephobia gives you the minified and gzipped size of any npm package. For the real picture (what each dependency costs in your actual bundle, after tree-shaking and deduplication), run a bundle analyzer against your build. npx source-map-explorer works on most bundles, and npx vite-bundle-visualizer works for Vite projects.

It has been revealed that for each candidate, find the platform feature that would replace it and check its Baseline status. The quickest way is webstatus.dev or the Baseline badge on the feature’s MDN page.

For each library with a platform replacement, go back to the framework: Is it Baseline-safe for your audience? What does the swap cost? Does the feature cover how you actually use the library? Most of your decisions will fall out of question 1 (check the feature’s status against your browserslist) and question 3 (check your own usage).

It has been revealed that for Widely available features, swap and move on. For Newly available ones, either confirm your audience is on modern browsers or guard the new code with a quick feature check and keep a fallback:.

That way you ship less code to the users who can run it, without breaking the ones who can’t.

Recent findings suggest that add the clusters up, and the picture is concrete. The internationalization cluster is around 14 KB gzipped, HTTP is around 17 KB, the UI primitives are around 24 KB, and the Lodash utilities are 8 KB or more depending on how much of the library you were shipping. For a typical mid-sized app, that’s somewhere between 60 KB and 90 KB gzipped of dependencies you can hand back to the platform, and more if you were shipping the full lodash or several of these libraries at once. (The uncompressed numbers are two to three times larger, which is what you’ll see in a bundle analyzer before gzip.).

I’ve chosen relatively lean packages for most of these features, but some individual packages could still be heavy. Your dialog package, for instance, could alone weigh as much as 50KB gzipped depending on what you’re using.

A few features are worth keeping an eye on over the next year, because they’ll open up further swaps:.

None of this is a one-time cleanup. The platform ships latest features constantly, and the gap between “you need a library for this” and “the browser does this” keeps closing. The habit worth building is small: once a quarter, run the audit. List your dependencies, check what’s now Baseline, and hand back what you can.

Pick one cluster from this article, open your package.json, and see how much of it the browser already does for you.

Breaking: Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the ‘turbulence and violence of our times’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
  • Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
  • In a recent development, curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

In a recent development, curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

Recent findings suggest that “The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik says. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”.

Industry observers note that with Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik says. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”.

These themes, Malik states, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

According to recent reports, through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

Sources indicate that “I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik claims. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”.

Sources indicate that the Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

According to recent reports, the Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

In a recent development, “We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik indicates. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”.

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

Recent findings suggest that “I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

Dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

The Zero-Day sci-fi corridor highlights an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

It has been revealed that that matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

You can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

With over 14 years of experience and deep expertise in API development, third-party tool integration, and scalable software solutions, Alexey specializes in … More about Alexey ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Isadora Agency who help enterprise brands and market leaders navigate digital, evolve profitably, and launch unforgettable websites, products, and campaigns. Thank you!

According to recent reports, when front-end developers and UX engineers are tasked with building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, or destructive, the industry instinct is almost always the same: reach for a physics engine. Frameworks like Matter.js, Cannon.js, or custom WebGL solutions have become the gold standard for creating immersive, gamified websites.

When our team at Isadora Agency set out to build Stress Release, a digital stress-relief squeeze toy designed to let burnt-out creatives smash, stretch, and distort animated UI characters, we initially explored that route. The goal was to build a highly tactile experience where every click yielded a satisfying, squishy reaction.

But as we began prototyping, we realized something crucial: Physics engines produce plausible motion, but in our case, the animators produced intentional motion.

It has been revealed that we didn’t need our characters to act like realistic rubber balls bouncing uncontrollably around a canvas. We needed them to react in very specific, highly designed ways. So, we scrapped the physics engine entirely.

In this article, we’ll break down how we built a real-time stress-relief squeeze toy without a single line of WebGL or Matter.js, relying entirely on programmatic Lottie state controls, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

Industry observers note that our core requirement for Stress Release was absolute deterministic control. Our animators had crafted bespoke .json Lottie files that required exact, frame-by-frame sequencing.

Recent findings suggest that for instance, our ‘mega squeeze’ reaction required a precise 181-frame build-up followed by a specific release sequence. To honor this design, we needed an architecture that wouldn’t overwrite the animators’ crafted keyframes with algorithmic approximations.

In a recent development, the tighter the click-feedback loop (click → squish → score), the more you need deterministic frame control. By choosing programmatic state control using Lottie’s native API, we ensured that the interaction layer acted as a flawless trigger for the animation layer.

According to recent reports, because our architecture relied on Lottie and the standard DOM, rendering is handled directly by the Lottie runtime, which plays the JSON-based vector animations as SVGs internally. We selected elements directly by ID and CSS class, driving their behavior using a combination of Lottie animation segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math.

Sources indicate that to achieve a deeply satisfying “tactile feel” upon hitting a character, we used radial input mapping. The first step was converting the click from page coordinates into the character’s local coordinate space.

Every click was measured against the character’s center point, then translated into score, feedback intensity, and explosion placement:.

Then we calculate the straight-line distance from the center of the click using the Pythagorean theorem:.

That single number drives everything: the score, the feedback intensity, and where the explosion animation appears:.

The result is a concentric zone system — a perfect circle of scoring rings around the character’s center, similar to a dartboard. The visual complexity of the Lottie SVG is completely irrelevant to hit detection; the hitbox is always a clean circle. Critically, the explosion Lottie animation is repositioned to (a, b) — the same vector used for scoring, so it always appears exactly where the player clicked. This spatial accuracy creates the tactile “I hit that” sensation entirely through math and DOM positioning.

According to recent reports, because the experience used DOM-managed SVG elements, desktop clicks and mobile taps could be handled directly through native event listeners. This avoided extra raycasting or coordinate remapping layers, while keeping the interaction model aligned with how the animations were rendered.

Since the game requires a visual reaction at a specific point, Lottie handles all the squish and bounce feelings internally through its animation curves. Each character has a defined set of animation sections (idle loops, reaction frames, and end states) stored as frame ranges. When a click lands, we jump directly to the exact segment that matches the current game state:.

On every click, we advance through the play order and fire the next segment:.

When the segment completes, control returns to the idle loop:.

And for the mega squeeze build-up, the bar loops on a specific frame range until triggered:.

Another major factor in our architectural decision was responsive behavior. Because we built Stress Release in the DOM, we bypassed the complexities of scaling bounding boxes and collision vectors across different devices.

It has been revealed that we handled responsive resizing entirely through CSS variables. By recalculating CSS custom properties on every resize, the layout simply reacts to the updated variables, and the Lottie SVGs scale naturally inside their containers without losing their state:.

While this architecture gave us total control over the art direction, it introduced a different challenge: file size.

According to recent reports, lottie JSON files can be heavy. We had 21 different character animations, plus multiple explosion variants that all needed to load. To ensure the experience remained fluid — especially on mobile devices — we implemented a few aggressive optimization strategies:.

When determining the stack for a gamified web experience, it is critical to let the design requirements dictate the technology.

Because our interactions required bespoke, highly controlled visual reactions, we opted for programmatic state control over emergent simulation. This decision empowered the animators to dictate the exact feel of the experience, leaving the code to do what it does best: listen, calculate, and trigger.

By mapping Lottie’s native timeline capabilities to the DOM, you can deliver incredibly rich, tactile user experiences while maintaining absolute control over the art direction.

New EU Guidelines For AI Labelling

📅 2026-08-13 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, there’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping newly introduced AI rules” in the EU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, there’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping newly introduced AI rules” in the EU. In reality, it’s a lot more narrow — and a lot more sensible. And mostly it’s about making AI more obvious when it actually needs to be obvious — especially for AI-generated content.

Sources indicate that starting from Aug 2, 2026, AI labelling is a legal requirement for any manufacturer that serves EU citizens. And similar to European Accessibility Act, it’s not limited to EU companies. It affects any company worldwide with EU operations as long as their AI output is used by people in the EU. Let’s see what exactly it means for us.

The goal of AI labelling is to help everyone exposed to AI content to recognize, in a clear and distinguishable way, that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

According to Article 50(4) of the AI Act, AI labelling applies to:.

It has been revealed that both providers (who build or supply the AI system) and deployers (who use it) carry legal obligations. Similar to GDPR and EAA, a manufacturer doesn’t escape Article 50 just because it licensed an external AI tool from a third party.

However, it doesn’t mean that all AI-generated content must be explicitly labelled.

Sources indicate that beyond the use cases above, pretty much everything else — the vast majority of AI-assisted work — simply isn’t covered by upcoming transparency rules. Most notably, the disclosure obligation does not apply where the AI-generated text has been reviewed and edited by a human, with a named person or entity taking editorial responsibility for it.

Sources indicate that some confusion circles around what exactly “public interest” means, where it starts and where it ends. On its own, it refers to health, safety, environment, economy, finances, politics, science, or culture. If AI-generated product claims touch upon them, the disclosure rule applies.

Industry observers note that some law firms recommend labelling realistic AI-generated illustrations or photos as a precaution for advertising, marketing and other commercial content. AI-generated product illustrations, photos, or posters do need a disclosure, as long as they resemble a real person, place, object, or event.

But at which point does edited AI content stop being AI content? When a form is pre-filled with AI, but then a user edits it, is it still AI? EU Commission’s guidance is a little fuzzy. Small assistive edits — spellcheck, grammar, formatting, cropping, colour correction, and AI-generated translation — don’t count as AI generation.

According to recent reports, AI-generated summaries, composite imagery, substantive rewrites, or adding and removing elements from a photo are considered AI generation. In practice, fine-tuning a sentence a person wrote is fine, but generating the sentence on its own requires a disclosure.

“A human skimmed it before publishing” doesn’t qualify as editorial review. The Commission is explicit that it needs to be substantive, with a named person responsible for the editorial control.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, the fine line lies between intentional manual intervention and automated generation. The latter always has to be disclosed (exception: closed B2B environments).

As part of the Code of Practice, the European Commission has published an EU AI icon set. It’s a specific “AI” mark (similar to the AI label in Carbon Design System) — not the generic ✨ sparkle that many products use to signal AI. The signal must be “clear and distinguishable”.

The sparkle might be too ambiguous to signal AI clearly. Mostly because it’s often used to mean “AI-powered feature”, rather than “this specific content was generated by AI”. That’s the kind of signal EU guidelines are trying to rule out.

The Commission is explicit: using an icon “does not establish legal compliance by itself.” A barely visible icon, a note buried in the footer, or a label that flashes for a second are all not compliant.

It has been revealed that the icon should be clearly visible, with a plain language label and accessible to assistive technologies. A safe bet is to pair any icon with plain text (“AI-generated”) — and it needs to persist when being reshared or downloaded.

In fact, the EU Commission also published Code of Practice on marking and labelling of AI content.

It might feel like a yet another regulation coming from the EU, but in reality there are plenty of other similar regulations that emerged recently worldwide:.

All of these are signs of upcoming AI regulation that looks more like a pattern, rather than a coincidence. So if you’re shipping anything AI this year, it’s probably a good idea to have a conversation about what exactly is going to be AI-labelled, and what not.

One final note is that new EU AI transparency rules are much broader than US laws on AI disclosure, where certain state laws require disclosures for synthetic human performers, political advertising or specific AI applications.

None of this really deserves panic or confusion. It’s about a fairly simple idea that has been emerging worldwide at almost the same time:.

If anything, it will help people distinguish between AI slop and not AI — and everybody can only benefit from that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a new auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.

Industry observers note that kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a latest auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).

It has been revealed that no. 3P.B. (1960) by Yayoi Kusuma. Courtesy Sotheby's.

According to recent reports, the 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.

Sources indicate that roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.

Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.

According to recent reports, one of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.

Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.

The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.

Roy Lichtenstein's Two Paintings Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983) Courtesy Sotheby's.

It was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.

It has been revealed that not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.

After the sale, Sotheby’s mentioned works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.

“When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, stated following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—states it all.”.

On Tuesday night, the Upcoming York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.
