We know that everything on the web is a box by default, but you’ll find many animated s pretending to be circles. But if you’ve ever met a real , you’ll know that they’ve got a lot more going for them. Dressed in SVG, they fit into a wider range of crowds than a humble wearing HTML/CSS can. has a strict no .html policy.

The tag is not as static as its name suggests. Any embedded JavaScript unfortunately won’t run if you load an SVG file with an tag, but CSS animations work perfectly fine. Many of the SVG attributes do have CSS property counterparts, and the geometry properties have been supported across the major browsers since 2024. Some attributes that you might want to animate, like viewBox, don’t have equivalents yet.

It has been revealed that besides JavaScript and CSS, there’s another way to animate SVGs: Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL). Despite its quirks, it’s still worth learning. Like CSS animations, SMIL animations also work in tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG, without JavaScript.

If you’ve never heard of SMIL or need a refresher, check out Andy Clarke’s well-named article. Then we’ll look at a way to plan an animation and make SMIL markup more manageable.

According to recent reports, SMIL has a problem: it gets bloated promptly. Unlike CSS and JavaScript, where you can list multiple properties in each keyframe and easily reuse animations, each SMIL tag can only target one element and only one property of that element at a time. A property can be animated through a list of values. But it is still one tag, one element, one property. The shortest way you can write a color and opacity change that will run is the following:.

That’s not bad, but consider that it needs to be repeated for every element included in the animation. A SMIL animation can promptly get longer than its CSS equivalent.

To make things easier when starting a new animation, let’s blueprint all of the elements and properties we want to animate, and create a list of descriptive IDs for each tag.

I like to plan my animations using what’s called a timing chart. A timing chart is effectively a line segment; some choose horizontal lines, others prefer vertical, which is a great analogy for animation as a whole because line segments can run parallel, overlap, and follow each other with or without a gap. Just like animations.

In a recent development, for now, we’re only interested in when animations start and stop. When drawing our charts, we’ll forget about the in-between lines and instead draw a line for each component animation, marking the beginning and end. I like to annotate timing with a circle and a bar. You can draw your chart using whatever, and it doesn’t have to be exactly to scale, as long as the relative timing between all the little animations that make up the whole is clear. Besides, adding labels for the durations is an easy cheat to get around drawing to scale.

Here is a demo of how I typically set up a timing chart with more than one animation:.

See the Pen [colorAndOpacityChange [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016dc-399c-7652-b172-4cd4663746b9) by Johan Grobler.

Industry observers note that the important thing to note is that the timing chart lines are arranged according to how the animations are arranged in time. One piece of the animation follows the next piece, which is followed by a subsequent piece, and so forth. It visualizes how the animation’s parts run together and cascade over time.

A major part of SMIL is synchronization. It’s even in the name, after all. And there are multiple ways to specify when an animation should start (here’s a test case to check what your browser supports). One of the most useful ways is with a syncbase value, which is a SMIL tag’s ID followed by either .begin or .end, with an optional positive or negative offset.

Sources indicate that let’s piggyback off the previous animation example that includes changes in color and opacity. If we want the opacity animation to start 300 milliseconds before the color animation finishes, we could do arithmetic. Alternatively, the second animation can use the syncbase value colorChange.end - 300ms. This way, the relative timing between the two animations becomes explicit.

It has been revealed that using syncbase values, the beginning of an animation is positioned in time relative to the .begin or .end of some other animation. A positive offset moves the start to the right (forwards in time), and a negative offset to the left (backwards in time).

See the Pen [syncbase.end [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/emgwwGJ) by Johan Grobler.

Industry observers note that something with negative offsets is that they can specify a time before the document has loaded or when a click happens. Computers can’t predict the future (at least not yet). The best they can do is jump the animation to where it would have been had the computer peeked into the future to preemptively start the animation. The second animation only runs from start to finish if there is enough room, so to speak.

See the Pen [syncbase.begin [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/xbgooXq) by Johan Grobler.

Recent findings suggest that syncbase values don’t only allow you to connect animations from .end to .begin. Elect a primary animation; the animation that first comes to mind is usually the best representation of the group. All secondary animations can be set with begin="primary.begin". I’ve only used the ID #primary for emphasis. That way, all the other animations begin relative to that starting point. Stacking animations like this reduces maintenance if, say, we later want the whole group to start at a different time.

It has been revealed that let’s put the idea to work and build a loading indicator (or spinner). Then we’re going to explore how changing the relative timing between the parts changes the effect of the whole animation:.

Recent findings suggest that browsers have wide support for the prefers-reduced-motion media feature and Val Head explains this in depth in another article. We definitely want to respect this user preference as we consider moving things around. In fact, consider it non-negotiable.

There are various approaches to adhering to a user’s prefers-reduced-motion setting when it comes to SMIL. Each with its pros and cons. Evaluating early on what’s going to work best for your use case could save you a partial rewrite down the line.

For example, we could consider using a element instead of a plain because supports multiple elements that can be used as fallbacks in a media attribute for reduced motion preferences.

Sources indicate that or one SVG file with an inline CSS @media query that uses display: none to swap between versions. That said, it’s an approach that might cause trouble in various environments. But browsers are continuously changing, and this might not be an glitch in the future.

You might also consider a CSS background-image instead because we can wrap that style in a media query — @media (prefers-reduced-motion) — that sets a static image as the fallback for reduced motion preferences.

According to recent reports, there are even more options we can turn to! For example, SVG’s element can also be used to swap things out for motion preferences.

Or, if we prefer everything bundled together, we can use JavaScript .matchMedia() and the handy SMIL DOM interface to control which animations start instead of completely switching out files.

For this, I’m avoiding any motion and sticking to opacity animations, which tend to cause less trouble. For a non-interactive animation like this, we can load it in an tag. When we add motion, we can go the route to show the most appropriate version of our animation.

We’re going to do our own version of the classic three-dot spinner:.

See the Pen [StaticDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016e5-c44d-75b3-bbb2-3eca2f83932d) by Johan Grobler.

SVG wizards might be able to do everything directly in a text editor. I recommend using a graphic editor like Inkscape if you’re having trouble visualizing how the markup will be rendered. Once again, Andy Clarke has a great article about his process for optimizing and structuring his own drawings.

It has been revealed that note: There’s a gotcha with Inkscape. Setting what you would expect to be an element’s ID via the Layers window actually sets the value of a metadata attribute used internally by Inkscape. Use Inkscape’s object properties or XML editor window to set the true element’s ID. Your mileage may vary with a different editor. Also, in Inkscape, remember to save the file as optimized SVG when the drawing is done to strip away unneeded metadata.

In a recent development, OK, so we’re sticking with the opacity animation idea. The dots are going to fade in and out. We’ll use separate tags for those. Six tags in total.

Our naming scheme is going to be straightforward: we’ll call them #fadeIn and #fadeOut, and to differentiate between each pair of tags, we’ll postfix the tag’s ID with either Left, Middle or Right. Try to follow a convention that makes sense to you when coming up with your own IDs.

The fade-in tag for the dot on the left:.

And the fade-out for the middle dot:.

We have an infinite number of ways in which we could space these six animations in time. Let’s look at a couple of choice examples alongside their timing charts to see how changing the arrangement of the parts impacts the visual effect of the whole animation.

To narrow our choices a bit, all of the tags will use the same dur value, and none of the syncbase values will have offsets.

For someone coming from a culture that reads from left to right, the dots appearing on screen along the same pattern would feel natural. Let’s also start with all the dots fading out together at the end:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion1 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ec-0b1b-731e-bf44-2dd45b7c075f) by Johan Grobler.

Syncbase values stagger the fade-ins and restart the loop when the dots have disappeared:.

It has been revealed that since all the fade-outs end at the same time, it is an arbitrary choice which one we use to restart the loop. We’ll consider #fadeOutLeft as the primary animation here and also synchronize the other fade-outs to it with the syncbase value fadeOutLeft.begin. Later, if we want to move the fade-outs in time, all we do is change when #fadeOutLeft starts.

Instead of a group fade-out, we could stagger them just like the fade-ins:.

Sources indicate that without adding an offset, there are a couple of points in time we could start #fadeOutLeft at. If it starts on fadeInRight.end:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion2 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ef-1be0-7359-a8ce-1d45194ed50a) by Johan Grobler.

The visual effect is subtly changed by moving up a spot and starting #fadeOutLeft on fadeInMiddle.end instead:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion3 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016ef-f4d9-745b-a89f-2ff35d898589) by Johan Grobler.

We can see from the charts that we could try moving up a spot further to fadeInLeft.end:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion4 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f1-07f8-732a-966d-c295618c60d7) by Johan Grobler.

How about starting the sequence with a fade-out:.

See the Pen [dotsVersion5 [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f1-b6a5-7078-a73c-217459f53e20) by Johan Grobler.

You might prefer to start with the dot in the middle:.

See the Pen [centerFirstDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f2-5f78-70a2-a948-f030c147fbe3) by Johan Grobler.

In a recent development, as you iterate on your animation, timing charts are a great way to keep track of your work, and they make visual comparison between versions possible. And by drawing a timing chart, you might even see a pattern in the timing between the parts of the animations that you might otherwise have missed.

Recent findings suggest that as you animate more elements and properties, it gets harder to keep track of what starts when. To see how timing charts can help you make sense of things, let’s build on the basic spinner:.

See the Pen [staticDotsWithClipPaths [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f4-f99c-7779-b526-1265ecf5619b) by Johan Grobler.

I’ve added a for each dot to the drawing. We’ll move those into to a tag and remove the fill="white". As the animation runs, the rectangles are going to move over the dots for a different approach to animating the stroke than by animating stroke-dashoffset.

We only need a single for all three dots, but it adds structure to the document, and it’s good practice to wrap it, and similar tags, in a tag:.

Industry observers note that remember to set the clip path for the s. Either with CSS or using the clip-path attribute:.

Because the dots now have a stroke added, to leave their size unchanged, we need to compensate by subtracting half the value of stroke-width from r:.

According to recent reports, that’s all the changes the graphics need. Have a look at the animated version with its timing chart, then we’ll look in more detail at the changes that have been made to the animation:.

See the Pen [clipPathDots [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f8-73b0-707a-b21a-7aa07fb194b2) by Johan Grobler.

There’s a new animation, #moveClipPathLeft, that starts the whole sequence, and to tweak the animation’s rhythm a bit, there’s a 1s delay between when the fade-outs end and the loop restarts:.

You could use s to move the rectangles instead, but we need to move them back to their starting positions at the end for a smooth restart of the animation. You’ll need to take into account which tags can animate and set which data types if you do decide to animate the transform attribute instead of translating the rectangles with the y attribute.

To change things up, the for the middle dot moves down:.

We’re also using the fill-opacity property instead of the opacity property for the fade-ins, and they’ve been synchronized to start once a dot’s clipping has finished moving:.

The fade-outs still use the normal opacity property, so both the fill and stroke fade out together. Because this arrangement is set up to use a group fade-out at the end, there are a few places the markup could be optimized. One of them is dropping the fill="freeze" to automatically reset the dot’s opacity back to its starting value once the tag finishes running:.

According to recent reports, for the tags that did use fill="freeze", we’ll use tags to reset those properties back to their starting values. I’ve simplified the chart a little by lumping those tags together. Because these tags don’t have a duration over which they act, on the chart I’ve drawn the start and end markers over each other.

To reset the fill-opacity on the left dot:.

If you use fill="freeze" with the fade-outs, you’ll need an extra for each dot to reset the middle dot’s opacity:.

According to recent reports, the last thing we need to do is move the clipping rectangles back to their starting positions. For the right :.

That’s just one of the possible timing variations, and most of what you’ll need to try some of the others, as we did with the basic spinner, is already in place. You might want to have a try at coming up with a couple of your own alternate timings.

To sum things up, we know that balancing the different stages of an animation can be difficult at best, and untenable at worst. Any time we get into multi-step animations that exceed one or two steps, it’s a form of orchestration. You’re almost building a Rube Goldberg machine of markup. And using a timing chart is a strategy I use that I hope will help you in your projects as well. They are outlines of what to expect and when, allowing you to map things out in a way that not only helps plan your code, but also makes future updates and maintenance a lot more bearable than going into it without a plan.

While a timing chart can’t reduce the complexity of the markup, it can give a good overview of what should happen when. Timing charts are definitely not limited to SMIL animations. Unfortunately, syncbase values are, and they can still help even if you’re going to use a different approach to implementing your animation.

According to recent reports, I highly recommend checking out Andy’s other articles on Smashing Magazine. There’s even more stuff on combining CSS and SVG.

Yosra Emad wrote a great article on creating animations with multiple steps in CSS, and you might want to try drawing a few timing charts as you read through it.

When you’re ready to start adding those in-between lines to your timing chart, Nash Vail’s article on easing dives deep into the details of easing curves.

You might also be interested in tests for your browser’s SVG implementation to see what is supported.

Industry observers note that four hands in ruffled lace cuffs and pink brocade sleeves reach in from the dark corners of the opening frame, crossing chrome flashlight beams over a stacked white wordmark. Early editions leaned on flip-books before annual resets explored time travel in 2024 and collecting in 2025. Starting from the classical musical nocturne, the Rotterdam duo recast Amsterdamâs 65-plus participating museums as an unscripted nighttime maze.

On the Prinsengracht canal column, that maze turns into a literal red thread. A crisp white top band locks black MUSEUM NACHT caps opposite the ZATERDAG 7 NOVEMBER 2026 date stamp, while white AMSTERDAM type drops straight into the dark scene below, linked across the border by a looping crimson line. Beneath that split header, a figure in a pleated collar and bright blue stockings floats mid-air beside giant silver keys and dark botanical leaves. A companion monochrome column swaps colour for a close-up portrait with closed eyes, orbited by a floating die, pocket watch, glass tumbler, fork, and bird ornament. #22931. Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s vital to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October.
  • Sources indicate that the previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

Industry observers note that “It’s vital to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

Sources indicate that the previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024.

According to recent reports, of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

It has been revealed that the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

In a recent development, the disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” stated Andrew Terner, a Latest York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

According to recent reports, but maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

It has been revealed that moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

According to recent reports, the ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

In a recent development, suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

According to recent reports, the following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” indicates Magnus Resch, a Fresh York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.).

According to recent reports, “It is vital for the public to visit an art fair,” indicates Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”.

Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

Industry observers note that collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

In a recent development, the card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the new card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card states something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

In a recent development, the system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

Scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

The physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the big figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image highlights what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch. It runs over your real code, lets your team edit anything visually, and puts agents to work on content, accessibility, and the maintenance you never get to. Incubated at Strapi. Thank you!

According to recent reports, every website is at its best the day it ships. The final branch merges, the site goes live exactly as designed, and it is briefly perfect. It will never be this good again.

Industry observers note that not because anything breaks. The site keeps working. But the market moves, the messaging shifts, a competitor launches something, and the careful thing you built slowly stops matching the company it represents. A year later, it is a period piece. Not broken, just behind. Every team knows this decay, and almost everyone treats it as a law of nature.

Industry observers note that it doesn’t have to be that way. A website could keep improving after launch instead of drifting away from its best day, quietly optimizing itself while the team that built it works on something else.

Picture it working: while you sleep, an agent catches that last week’s design-system change never propagated to the pricing page, and fixes it. Another finds a set of images shipped uncompressed in a rushed release and optimizes them. A third flags an accessibility regression a new component introduced, and either fixes it or leaves it for you to check. You wake up to a site that is measurably better than the one you left, and a short list of the few decisions the agents wanted your eyes on. That is the version worth wanting.

And the moment you take that promise seriously, you run into a problem that has nothing to do with the technology:.

Sources indicate that the obvious move, once you have capable agents, is to hand them the whole site. Let them write, edit, optimize, and publish, and get out of the way. It sounds like the natural endpoint, and it is the first thing most people picture when they hear “autonomous website.”.

It is also the thing almost nobody wants once it is real in front of them.

We learned this the way you learn most things worth knowing: by building the opposite first. Building Fimo, an autonomous website platform, we set out to make websites fully autonomous, assumed that was the goal, and then watched what people actually did with it. What they did was hesitate. Not because they distrusted the agents, but because a website has no single owner. Different parts belong to different people, and each one wants a different amount of autonomy. So the question was never whether to trust the agents. It was where to draw the line, and for whom.

Once you ask it that way, the work splits cleanly into three kinds.

Sources indicate that start with the largest pile, because it is bigger than people expect. Most of what keeps a website healthy is rule-bound, repetitive, and completely joyless. Keeping accessibility compliant as pages change. Propagating a design-system enhancement once a token moves. Catching a broken meta tag, an unoptimized image, a link that rotted when a URL changed three sprints ago.

According to recent reports, none of this is where anyone’s talent lives. Nobody was hired because of their gift for spotting a missing alt attribute. This is the work you are actively relieved to hand off, and it is the work agents are best at, because it is defined by rules rather than taste. An agent that quietly keeps this layer correct across a whole site, unattended, is not a threat to anyone’s job. It is the tedious eighty percent finally taken care of.

Industry observers note that naming how much of the maintenance load actually lives in this pile is what makes the whole idea of an autonomous site feel less like a leap. You are not handing over judgment. You are handing over chores.

At the other end sits the work you would not delegate at any price. It is a small pile, but it is the reason you exist.

Recent findings suggest that an agent can check a newly introduced page against every rule you have given it. It can confirm the contrast passes, the heading order is right, the tokens are correct, the copy matches the style guide. What it cannot do is decide what the page should feel like, or whether the thing you are shipping is, in the taste sense, good. That judgment is exactly what you were hired for, and no amount of capability moves it off your desk.

This is the part people reach for first when they resist autonomy, and they are right to protect it. The mistake is thinking the whole site is made of this kind of work. Almost none of it is. But that small part matters more than all the rest, which is why automating everything feels so wrong.

Between the chores and the untouchable sits the part no product can settle for you, because the line runs through different places for different people.

Recent findings suggest that notice what is happening there. It isn’t that one of them is cautious and the other reckless. It is that the same task carries different amounts of judgment for each of them. For one person it is a decision; for the other it is a chore. There is no default a product could ship that would be right for both, because “right” is a function of where your value sits, not of the task itself.

Sources indicate that this is why the control has to be per-task and per-person, and why we stopped trying to find the setting that would work for everyone. There isn’t one. There is only the line each person draws, and the tools to draw it precisely.

Recent findings suggest that once you accept that the line is personal, a toggle between “approve” and “delegate” stops being enough. Where the line sits depends on what the agent is actually doing, so the real unit of control is the agent itself.

Recent findings suggest that this is where it stopped being a settings problem, and it is the shape Fimo took. You don’t pick from a fixed menu of behaviors. You compose the agents, deciding what each one is even allowed to touch. You can build one from scratch, or take one close to your needs and shape it to your own line: an accessibility agent you trust to run unattended, a content agent you keep close to anything brand-facing.

And they don’t stay fixed. They learn from their tasks and from what you teach them, so the boundary you set last month isn’t the one you’re stuck with. What you had to approve then, you can delegate now, not because you lowered your guard but because the agent earned it. The line is not a setting you configure once. It moves as trust is earned, in the direction of less work for you.

In a recent development, none of this means flipping a site to autonomous on day one. In practice it goes the other way. You delegate a little, watch how it does, and loosen.

And you can actually watch. Every agent’s runs, its history, its logs, and a before-and-after of what it changed are there to inspect. Trust doesn’t grow because you got used to the idea; it grows because you can see what happened and compare. The first time an agent quietly fixes something you would have missed, and you can see exactly what it did, the next delegation gets easier.

Sources indicate that deadlines keep you from becoming the bottleneck on what you have already handed over. If you don’t weigh in, the agent proceeds. You set the terms once, and you stop being the thing the whole site waits on.

It has been revealed that the worry people voice first is that an agent will change something on their site without them. Turn it around: the real risk is a site that never changes at all. A frozen site doesn’t stay safe. It just falls behind, slowly, in a way nobody notices until it represents a tech giant that no longer exists.

In a recent development, the point of autonomy was never to remove you from your website. It was to remove the decay.

In a recent development, the point of autonomy is to keep the launch-day version from being the best version, and to let you spend your judgment on the handful of things that actually deserve it, while the rest takes care of itself. Draw the line where your value is. Let the agents hold everything on the other side of it. And let the line move as they prove they can.

In a recent development, imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots.

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee.

In a recent development, most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock.

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

Industry observers note that what makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an crucial redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Sources indicate that head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Industry observers note that before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

In a recent development, in the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

According to recent reports, return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:.

Industry observers note that hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.

Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

According to recent reports, the Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

In a recent development, the Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

It has been revealed that now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

Do: Stack Hyatt's 5th Night Free Benefit.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations.

Recent findings suggest that hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Massive Sur), availability at standard rates disappears promptly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

Do: Combine With Chase Ultimate Rewards.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

According to recent reports, bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum.

Recent findings suggest that this is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value.

According to recent reports, category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards.

Industry observers note that hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

According to recent reports, this isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

In a recent development, this redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. #22926. Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In organisations today, data has never been more available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently. Her background in … More about Meriem ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction.

In a recent development, when that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all.

Data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional.

For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you.

It has been revealed that in 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different.

Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal.

But visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative. The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about?

Industry observers note that one of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics. Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline.

Industry observers note that before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss.

Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio: every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal.

Industry observers note that for a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context, under specific pressure. Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is.

Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it.

Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart.

That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on.

The high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project.

It has been revealed that most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible.

Defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric, a population, and an implied action. That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely.

It has been revealed that starting with available data produces a dashboard that answers no particular question, because it was never built for one — every number is present, none of them pointed anywhere. Starting with the operational question does the reverse: every element on the screen earns its place, because each one is there to help answer it.

In a recent development, for example, consider a UX team trying to fix a leaky checkout flow for an e-commerce website. A data-first approach pulls everything available, from clicks to scroll depth and device types, yielding a massive dashboard that leaves everyone asking, “Okay, but what do we actually change?” A context-first approach starts with a constraint: “At which step of the checkout do users drop off?” By filtering out 90% of the noise, the team builds a simple funnel chart, instantly spots a bottleneck on the payment screen, and knows exactly what to redesign.

Designing for an audience comes down to two things: accountability and familiarity.

According to recent reports, familiarity is about data literacy. Do they read charts instinctively, or does a complex visualisation create friction? Handing a dense, multi-layered dashboard to a Head of Sales and a senior analyst is like giving the same map to someone who navigates by landmarks and someone who reads grid coordinates. The data is accurate, but it is only functional for one of them.

In a recent development, accountability dictates how that complexity must be presented. A chart showing a 12% decline carries vastly different weight for the executive responsible for that number versus the analyst simply reporting it. Understanding your audience means grasping this relationship; data is never processed neutrally when your performance is on the line.

Together, familiarity and accountability decide one practical thing: how much you can put in front of someone.

In data visualisation, simplicity is not a fixed virtue — the right level of it is contingent on who is reading, and what they need to do.

An analyst relies on a high-density environment to conduct diagnostic discovery. By isolating individual behaviour nodes and mapping out raw user flows, they interrogate the data at its atomic level to uncover the hidden insights and underperforming spend that will shape future campaigns.

An executive, by contrast, requires a highly synthesised translation of that data to immediately identify what is driving commercial growth. Tailoring a dashboard to your audience means adjusting the density dial, delivering maximum signal with appropriate complexity for the specific brain in the room.

According to recent reports, most data projects operate on the comfortable assumption that if a chart is accurate and clear, the insight will take care of itself. In reality, information and insight are entirely different states. Information is what the data indicates, whereas insight is the specific decision, shift in understanding, or course correction someone makes as a result of seeing it. If the intended business change isn’t defined before the design begins, a dashboard will default to passive reporting rather than driving action.

Marketing and engineering teams experience the danger of this gap whenever a core business metric suddenly plummets.

Industry observers note that A dashboard built for information simply sounds the alarm, showing a chart that tracks a sharp 15% drop in booking rates. Because the data lacks depth, leadership defaults to panic: they immediately call the UX design team, assuming the app is broken or the checkout flow is flawed. Because the data doesn’t pinpoint the core of the problem, it triggers a costly, misplaced fire drill.

Recent findings suggest that A dashboard built for insight isolates the variables required to make an informed decision. Instead of a single, flat booking metric, the visualisation maps the drop against traffic sources and campaign releases — instantly revealing that while app performance and core user conversion are perfectly stable, the sitewide rate was artificially diluted by a massive influx of low-intent click traffic from a newly scaled campaign. The team doesn’t waste time redesigning a functioning app; they get the exact insight needed to pause the underperforming marketing campaign and adjust their acquisition strategy.

Every visualisation implies a next step, even if that step is “nothing needs to change right now.” The question is whether the design makes that implication clear enough for the viewer to recognise it.

It has been revealed that my aha moment in data visualisation happened during a project for a client-facing B2B SaaS platform focused on enterprise talent management and competency tracking in Pegasystems skills. The platform captured a massive footprint of daily telemetry, and the brief arrived open-ended: “We have an immense archive of user activity, now we need to present it to enterprise teams.”.

We could very easily have charted everything that was captured, but we wouldn’t be doing end users any favours if they just ended up looking at a data graveyard. My responsibility immediately moved beyond pure interface craftsmanship; it became about architecting a highly practical tool for real people who would open this dashboard routinely and need it to tell them an honest, immediate story about their workflows.

Here is how the project actually went.

According to recent reports, the client believed this massive pool of data could help their customers perform better, and wanted an interface that finally enabled that growth. Translating that broad ambition into tangible visualisations required defining the practical mechanics of performance. What variables indicate advancement vs passive usage? What does “perform better” actually mean? How do you measure it?

According to recent reports, an obvious candidate was time spent by product. Every platform tracks it. It is easy to show, and it feels meaningful. But time spent is a proxy; it tells you someone was there, not whether they got anything out of it.

In a recent development, the more meaningful signals were competency scores by area, certification completion rates, and historical performance trajectories. Integrating time-spent data alongside these performance metrics added a useful layer of interpretation, helping us surface which modules users were underutilising and whether that directly correlated with lagging scores. Time spent became a supporting signal in the larger story.

The second question was about the appropriate level of granularity. An identical metric carries completely different weight depending on who is looking at it. An individual contributor tracking their own completion rate needs to know if they are pacing correctly, whereas a manager reviewing a team aggregate needs to know precisely who requires immediate support. This distinction shaped every subsequent data-exposure and filtering decision. Defining that structural story early determined exactly what to show, and to whom.

The most straightforward approach to this design would have been predictable: use the same charts, but offer an individual view and an aggregated team view. Far too many dashboards rely on this shortcut, subtly tweaking the scale of identical data visualisations and labelling it “personalisation.”.

An authentic analysis of the audience reveals a much deeper rift. Frontline team leads and individual contributors required distinct narrative structures and design principles.

Sources indicate that having used e-learning platforms myself, I remember the frustration of opening a tool without a clear sense of my current standing, core strengths, or slipping metrics. That personal experience directly guided the individual contributor workspace; it needed to act as a highly tailored, self-directed mirror that was granular, honest, and personal.

Conversely, the manager’s interface had to bypass individual milestones initially to provide a macro pulse check on team vulnerabilities. It was designed around a different operational reality: how is the group progressing, and where are the consistent gaps? The view prioritised the aggregate picture first, while retaining an intuitive path to drill down into tactical day-to-day coordination when needed.

Industry observers note that our insight strategy was locked in during the early conceptual phase, long before wireframing a single chart. We intentionally abandoned the idea of building a dense, passive data log and focused on pacing the narrative arc.

For individual contributors, the core value was self-direction, ensuring they could glance at the interface on a Monday morning and immediately derive a clear priority list for the week ahead.

For managers, the goal was to fundamentally shift the timing of operational conversations, providing them with the necessary baseline to intervene before a skill gap evolved into a critical project failure. The visualisations needed to surface the exact moments when a human check-in would be useful, shifting their workflow from reactive post-mortems to proactive guidance.

According to recent reports, the comparison tool was the highlight nobody had asked for. A manager dashboard and an individual dashboard are easy to anticipate. What is harder to land is: what if a manager wants to compare two specific team members against the same metrics, side by side? That view came from a design assumption, and it turned out to be the feature that resonated most.

The decisions that mattered most in this project weren’t in the initial brief — capturing data they hadn’t thought to request, and structuring it to answer questions they had not previously known how to articulate, which is the core differentiator of a user-centric data strategy.

The choice of visualisation layout must follow the geometric nature of the data itself. For this project, the core design problem was enabling an individual user to answer a specific question at a single glance: across eight distinct competency areas, where are my relative strengths and gaps?

It has been revealed that to solve this, we mapped the data using a radar chart. By organising multiple variables across axes radiating from a central point using polar coordinates, the interface connects the data points to form a single, unified shape. An even, balanced polygon instantly signals well-rounded proficiency, while a sharply skewed shape draws the eye immediately to an outlier area.

Industry observers note that while a traditional linear bar chart would have forced the viewer to scan eight individual bars and mentally calculate the variance, a concentric, radial layout segments the data layers to make progress tracking and skill gaps immediately readable. When all dimensions share an identical scale and scoring method, the radar chart is not an unconventional aesthetic choice — it is the most functional tool for multi-dimensional analysis.

The colour system was the other decision made early, and I mean early. During the branding exercise, each of the three products was assigned a colour. That colour did not stay in the brand guidelines. It was built into the data model from the beginning, running consistently across every chart, every filter, every breakdown. By the time a user landed on the dashboard for the first time, the mental model was already in place. They had not been taught the language. They already knew it.

The shift from passive information to active insight showed up first in how the dashboard was actually used. Following the deployment of the personalised dashboards and side-by-side team comparison tools, weekly active engagement on the platform’s analytics features rose noticeably, per internally reported figures. Managers were no longer opening the tool once a month to pull static reports. They were using it every Monday morning to actively plan their week.

According to recent reports, revenue and user growth also moved in the right direction over the following two quarters, though — as with most single-project outcomes — it’s hard to isolate the dashboard’s exact contribution from everything else that changed at the same time. The client reported churn across the platform falling to one of its lowest points on record. The clearest evidence of impact came from qualitative feedback. Managers reported that instead of using data to dissect a ‘bad’ month after the fact, the visualisations allowed them to instantly spot slipping performance and schedule a quick supportive catch-up before it turned into a real gap.

Data design reaches its full potential when visual presentation is treated as an upstream architectural choice rather than a downstream formatting step. Bringing structured UX thinking to data turns visualisations into active decision-making engines, ensuring every chart, report, and metric directly serves a human purpose:.

The next time you are tasked with creating a data visualisation — whether it is an enterprise dashboard, an executive report, or a public-facing infographic — step away from the design canvas and BI tools. Focus your initial effort on the human decisions behind the screen. Only then will your data stop being a passive log of the past and start driving the direction of the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

Recent findings suggest that the philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

In a recent development, the Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and right now serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

Recent findings suggest that the current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are upcoming to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn states, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

Industry observers note that the MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

In a recent development, during her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.
