Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party.
  • Sources indicate that hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions.
  • According to recent reports, hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most vital artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

Sources indicate that hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a new dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

According to recent reports, hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most important museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a fresh institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Industry observers note that raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

According to recent reports, produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)Hungarian National GallerySzent György térIn Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

Recent findings suggest that working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s new Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

According to recent reports, left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

It has been revealed that the Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most crucial artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

Judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareGoya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.

In a recent development, an apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Recent findings suggest that can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)Id. Antall József rkpIn the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

Comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939).

© Museum of Fine Arts – Vasarely Museum, Budapest.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)Vasarely Museum BudapestSzentlélek térFor the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

In a recent development, pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

It has been revealed that pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ Square.

It has been revealed that hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.

A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996).

Photo © József Rosta / Ludwig Museum - MoCA, Budapest.

© SUMUS Gáyor & Maurer Foundation.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)Ludwig MuseumKomor Marcell utcaDuring the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.

A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

Alaska Mileage Blueprint → JAL Business Class

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales.
  • Industry observers note that use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

In a recent development, earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Industry observers note that use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

It has been revealed that verify your target flight operates a Boeing 787 or 777 with JAL's "Sky Suite" business class product. Older aircraft on some routes may have a less desirable cabin configuration. Check SeatGuru or JAL's fleet page.

Phone Alaska's award desk at 1-800-252-7522. Have your dates, route, and JAL flight number ready. The agent will search their system and process the redemption. Expect $25-$50 in taxes and fees.

Recent findings suggest that picture this: you board a Japan Airlines Boeing 787-9 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, turn left, and settle into your own private suite. The JAL Sky Suite III closes around you — a fully flat bed, a sliding privacy door, direct aisle access from every seat. A flight attendant in a crisp kimono-inspired uniform takes your drink order before pushback. You're cruising at 35,000 feet over the Pacific in a cabin that feels more like a boutique hotel than an airplane, and you paid for it with points you earned on everyday spending. That's the experience this redemption delivers — and the math behind it is what makes the ChooseFI community absolutely love it. A JAL Business Class ticket from Seattle (SEA) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) typically retails between **$5,000 and $10,000** in cash. That's a real number — pull up JAL.com on any given date and you'll see it. Yet Alaska Mileage Strategy prices this exact award at just **60,000 miles** one way. On a $5,000 ticket, that's **8.3 cents per point**. On a $10,000 ticket — which is common during peak travel periods — that's a staggering **16.7 cents per point**. The ChooseFI benchmark for a "good" redemption is typically 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This blows past that by a factor of five to ten. Why does this gap exist? Because Alaska Mileage Plan uses a **fixed award chart** to price partner redemptions. They set the JAL Business Class rate years ago and haven't moved it in step with rising cash fares. As international business class prices have climbed, the points cost has stayed anchored — and that's the pricing inefficiency that savvy travelers exploit. This isn't a loophole that disappears tomorrow. JAL and Alaska have a deep, long-standing partnership. Alaska has consistently maintained this pricing as one of the crown jewels of its partner award chart. For anyone building toward financial independence who also wants to see the world in comfort, this redemption represents exactly what the FI travel rewards philosophy is about: using the system's own rules to access experiences that cash-wealthy people pay enormous sums for, nearly free.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Alaska's Fixed Award Chart Is the Key.

In a recent development, most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Strategy has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

Industry observers note that this creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Sources indicate that here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Strategy charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy Is Your On-Ramp.

Industry observers note that alaska Mileage Initiative has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most crucial nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

Industry observers note that the more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Initiative never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

The Routing Rules Bonus: Free Stopovers.

Recent findings suggest that alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Industry observers note that book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

It has been revealed that before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

It has been revealed that you need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Proposal miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Recent findings suggest that initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Proposal at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:.

It has been revealed that tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Industry observers note that before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

According to recent reports, if your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and Latest York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

In a recent development, let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Route: Seattle (SEA) → Tokyo Narita (NRT) on JAL Flight 009, operated by a Boeing 787-9.

In a recent development, the Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

Recent findings suggest that the Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

You check in at Seattle's dedicated JAL Business Class counter — no line, expedited security. You access the Alaska Lounge (or the JAL lounge on the international side, if available at your airport). At boarding, you turn left into the 787's Business Class cabin and find your JAL Sky Suite III: a fully enclosed suite with a sliding privacy door, a 43-inch seat that converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed, a 24-inch HD monitor, and dedicated storage. The seat has direct aisle access — you never have to climb over a seatmate.

In a recent development, JAL's inflight service is consistently ranked among the best in the world. The meal service features both Western and Japanese options, sake and premium spirits, and attentive crew who seem genuinely delighted to serve you. The 9–10 hour flight to Narita passes in quiet, restful comfort. You arrive refreshed.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Recent findings suggest that alaska's booking window opens 331 days before departure. For cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and Golden Week (late April through early May), JAL Business Class award space is competitive. Set a calendar reminder and search on JAL.com starting at day 335 — then call Alaska the moment the window opens if you see available seats.

It has been revealed that alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program. On a US-to-Japan routing, you could stop in Tokyo for four or five days, then continue to Osaka or another Japanese city (on a separate ticket), effectively getting a multi-city Japan trip from a single 60,000-mile award. Discuss this with the Alaska agent when booking.

Given Alaska's limited transfer partners, the most reliable path to a large Alaska miles balance is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card, which regularly offers welcome bonuses of 40,000–75,000 miles. Stack two cardholders in your household — you and your partner each earn a welcome bonus — and you have a round-trip business class redemption funded almost entirely from sign-up offers.

According to recent reports, marriott-to-Alaska transfers take 1 to 5 days and are irreversible. Never initiate the transfer until you've confirmed the award space exists on JAL.com. Transferring speculatively and then discovering the seat is gone is a painful and costly mistake.

It has been revealed that while JAL does release excellent inventory — hence the availability score of 4 out of 5 — "year round" availability doesn't mean unlimited. Japanese holidays (Golden Week, Obon in August, Latest Year's) see compressed availability. The best open inventory is typically September through November and January through mid-February.

In a recent development, alaska's policy is no fuel surcharges on partner awards, but always verify the final tax-and-fee total before giving your credit card number. Your total out-of-pocket should be well under $200 per ticket. If it's higher, ask the agent to itemize.

Recent findings suggest that this redemption is built for the ChooseFI couple or solo traveler who has been intentionally accumulating Alaska miles — or Marriott Bonvoy points — and wants to experience transpacific Business Class without the $8,000 price tag. If Japan is on your bucket list and you're willing to do a phone call to complete the booking, this is one of the highest-value redemptions in the entire loyalty ecosystem.

Minimum points needed: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. A couple needs 120,000 miles for two one-way Business Class tickets.

In a recent development, this redemption is rated **moderate** — and that rating is honest. It's not beginner-friendly (rated 2 out of 5 for beginners), but it's absolutely achievable for anyone willing to learn the two-step process. **What makes it moderate:** First, earning Alaska miles is less straightforward than earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex points. Alaska has **no direct credit card transfer partners** in the major bank ecosystems, which means you can't funnel everyday Amex or Chase spend into Alaska miles directly. You're relying on Alaska co-branded credit cards or the Marriott Bonvoy transfer path. Second, partner award bookings **cannot be completed online** — you must call Alaska Mileage Strategy. For travelers accustomed to booking everything digitally, this feels like friction. In practice, the call takes 15–20 minutes with a prepared agent and is genuinely straightforward. Third, while availability is rated 4 out of 5 (excellent by transpacific standards), you still need to plan ahead, particularly for peak Japan travel seasons. **Three tips to make it easier:** 1. **Start with the Alaska Airlines Visa card** — it's the most direct route to a large Alaska miles balance and regularly offers competitive welcome bonuses. 2. **Do your availability research on JAL.com before calling** — walk into that phone call with the flight number, date, and cabin class already confirmed. The booking becomes a five-minute transaction. 3. **Book 6–10 months out** for peak dates — this eliminates most of the availability stress and gives you time to transfer points if needed. If you've already booked one partner award by phone with any airline, this will feel familiar. If this is your first, the effort is absolutely worth it for a redemption worth 8–17 cents per point.

No. Alaska Mileage Plan is not a transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards. Your primary earning paths are the Alaska Airlines credit card, Marriott Bonvoy transfers, and purchasing miles during Alaska's periodic sales.

No. JAL flights booked with Alaska miles do not carry fuel surcharges. You will pay only government taxes and fees, typically $25-$50 for a one-way transpacific ticket. This is a major advantage over booking through some other programs.

The best availability appears right at the 331-day booking window. Shoulder seasons like January-February and September-November tend to have more open seats. Cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and summer are the most competitive periods.

Sources indicate that marriott Bonvoy points transfer to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. For every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred, you receive 20,000 Alaska miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus, totaling 25,000 Alaska miles. To reach 60,000 Alaska miles, you would need approximately 135,000 Bonvoy points (factoring in the bonus on each 60K tranche).

Recent findings suggest that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Alaska Mileage Plan to JAL business class is one of the best-kept sweet spots in travel rewards. At 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges, you get access to a world-class cabin at roughly half the mileage cost of competing programs. The earning path is narrower than programs with multiple transfer partners, but for anyone willing to build Alaska miles intentionally, the 8-13 cents per mile value on JAL business class to Japan is extraordinarily difficult to beat.

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • The mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for substantial works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • In a recent development, for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers remarked that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

The mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for substantial works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

In a recent development, for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” said Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a newly introduced buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

According to recent reports, in the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

In a recent development, subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” said the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

It has been revealed that with India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox said this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

Also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that demonstrated at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (Upcoming York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

According to recent reports, several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

By and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which demonstrated small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

Sources indicate that while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff said she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

The gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff noted.

Sources indicate that speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery showed a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he said.

Industry observers note that the gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

As many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan said, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

In a recent development, meanwhile, complications of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

It has been revealed that india's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of new Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

Industry News: Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December.
  • In a recent development, in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?
  • “We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a recent development, in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

It has been revealed that the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

According to recent reports, those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

In a recent development, and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch indicates the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

Sources indicate that “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She aims to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto notes, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

Recent findings suggest that for the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”.

The Filmmakers Behind ‘Primetime’ Printed the Entire Movie on 16mm and Rescanned It

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.
  • One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.
  • Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.

One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.

Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.

Recent findings suggest that the crew used London-based Cinelab, which has a third-generation 16mm Cine-Mitchell recorder built in-house. Once the film print was created, it was scanned back into digital using an Arriscan, which delivers “perfect edge-to-edge focus.” The resulting footage was then regraded.

It has been revealed that “Primetime is also a period film, in a way, and working with the film print helped make the visuals far more immersive,” says Bolen. “Any feeling of artifice in the image seemed to disappear after printing to film.”.

However, the film wasn’t shot entirely with the digital-to-film-to-digital method: Oppenheim and Bolen utilized a few obscure, frankly bizarre, cameras as they searched for a way to recreate that early 2000s aesthetic and also communicate the plot to the audience.

Industry observers note that one such camera was a 2005 MiniDV camera, the Panasonic AG DVX 100B. Bolen used this for the hidden camera shots, and it is a very similar technology that was used to film the original show, To Catch a Predator.

In a recent development, “These cameras are a challenge, because unlike modern cinema cameras, they can’t shoot in a LOG color space,” Bolen says. “We didn’t really alter their baseline settings; we decided to lean into the cameras’ built-in contrast. To Catch a Predator has such a strong look, and we tried to match it as closely as possible in-camera. Even in the final grade, we made very few adjustments.”.

But that distinct look posed a problem in the editing room: how to blend the shots taken by different cameras together. After all, DV cameras are not cinematic.

“We couldn’t get them to match,” claims Bolen on the Mark Bone YouTube channel. “Like, no matter what we did with the settings, some would skew red, some would skew green, on some the exposure seemed off.”.

According to recent reports, but Oppenheim didn’t care and threw the rules out of the window. In fact, he would film the same scenes on different cameras, and then in the edit, choose whichever one he liked.

Speaking of other cameras, there were two more that Oppenheim and Bolen used: a Plumbicon tube camera and a medical camera — the kind used for colonoscopies.

Archer Green points out that the Plumbicon tube camera actually dates back to the 1980s.

“It was meant to serve as a ‘spiritual’ camera rather than a period-accurate one,” Bolen writes for American Cinematographer. “These cameras use vacuum RGB tubes that split light into red, green, and blue, and the beautiful thing is that the tubes age and burn out over time. In a way, it’s a camera that feels like it has a soul — it decays over time, just like a human does.”.

The creators of ‘PRIMETIME’ explain how they shot a scene using a 480p colonoscopy camera 🎥🤯https://t.co/Z8m4aT7YM0.

— Complex Pop Culture (@ComplexPop) September 27, 2026.

For one of the close-ups of Pattinson, Bolen used a doctor’s colonoscopy camera. The crew even built a rig to hammer home the effect.

“That was a scary one because that camera does shoot 480p and I was like, ‘How am I going to get this approved?’ But to A24’s credit [the film distributor], they were like, ‘this is awesome’,” Bolen says.

“There are no rules. We don’t have to shoot 6K. 480p looks awesome on the major screen; I love it. It’s my favorite part of the movie.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

Industry observers note that the old mark was a tree in a circle, and it mentioned too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The new mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit shows something new.

The wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

This is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that indicates the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

Sources indicate that the floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that halide has announced version 3.4, much of which focuses on optimizations for the iPhone Duo. This includes a latest “XL” mode that is designed for two-handed operation, as well as a feature that doesn’t avoid the crease, but instead embraces it.

Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Halide says this feature, called XL mode, allows for “powerful two-handed operation.”.

“On the outer screen, we’ve added a few upcoming modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill. In low-light, the latter gives you a softer alternative to the built-in flash,” Halide adds.

“While apps like Apple’s own camera app expand the viewfinder to take up the full screen, it’s impossible to do this without obstructing your shot with camera controls. That poses a challenge when composing shots, so we’ve taken the approach of keeping the viewfinder clean.”.

Beyond just making these changes that take advantage of the two form factors the Duo offers, Halide went one step further and specifically engineered an interface for when the Duo is half-folded. The company claims that while most are avoiding the crease that appears when the phone is folded, it went the opposite way and embraced it.

“Back when the iPhone X debuted in 2017, we were the first app to ’embraced the notch’ by putting histograms in the ears of the phone. Today, we think we’re the first app to ’embrace the crease,’ placing the histograms in the fold, an otherwise no-man’s-land of interactions,” Halide says.

By default, Halide’s camera controls sit on the same side as the camera itself. Tapping the arrows in the sidebar, the left and right sides swap, turning Halide into a waist level viewfinder.

Halide provided a few sample images taken with the updated Duo app:.

It has been revealed that halide usually doesn’t take long to enhancement its app when latest hardware lands, and even though the interface for this Duo-specific update feels like it should have taken a lot longer, it really isn’t too far off from what Halide provided for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro launch. When it dropped version 3.2, which gave support for variable aperture control, that arrived on October 2, which is about three weeks after the iPhone 18 Pro landed on store shelves. This update for the Duo comes just shy of a month after the Duo rolled out on October 23.

Halide version 3.4 is available starting today.

Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record.
  • But the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates.
  • Recent findings suggest that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Newly introduced York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

But the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in New York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Recent findings suggest that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Newly introduced York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

In a recent development, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

Sources indicate that estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

It has been revealed that soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s Fresh York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

Sources indicate that the top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Sources indicate that harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

It has been revealed that one of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Mary Cassatt also established a fresh auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ACDSee Photo Studio has announced version 27, which brings a bunch of latest features, including several powered by AI, perhaps elevating the tool to the level of Adobe’s offerings.

Version 27 of the photo management and editing software for macOS introduces generative AI tools for creating and editing images, along with AI-powered organization that the manufacturer says can find and group photos together by how they look. These new options don’t compromise non-destructive editing, either.

In short, ACDSee has embraced AI editing.

“AI is shaping the future of photography and it’s our goal to lead the way in that space,” Frank Lin, CTO of ACD Systems, notes. “With ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27, we’re bringing generative AI directly into the creative process, making it easier to find, organize and transform images while giving photographers the flexibility and control they need to bring their vision to life.”.

The bulk of the updates to version 27 are AI-focused, with the top-billed latest feature having the highest chance of being the most controversial: image generation.

In a recent development, “Turn a text prompt into an image, choose a preset visual effect, or bring in reference images to guide character, style, and composition, right inside the photo workflow,” ACDSee says. AI generation isn’t new for photography tools, as Photoshop has had it for years now, but it’s not necessarily something that photographers are specifically asking for in a Lightroom competitor. Still, it’s here now.

ACDSee appears to be following Adobe’s lead with the next feature, as it now supports editing via prompting. Photographers can describe a change in plain language or “use reference images to guide the look, and reshape a photo without a single brush stroke.”.

Recent findings suggest that the AI search tool looks to be an alternative to Excire Photo and will find photos visually related to any primary target, with no keywords or tagging required. Images can also be grouped by similarity.

ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27 is available for $119.99, including 10,000 AI Credits for generative AI tools and 100GB of cloud storage.

#22853. This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (394 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (394 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.
  • HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment.
  • Industry observers note that meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. Consumers can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

The app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

Industry observers note that hyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

Lightning triggers are not a new concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

Lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

Industry observers note that however, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

#22850. Industry News: Apple’s Camera and Photo Software Lead Jon McCormack Has Retired

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (487 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Apple’s Camera and Photo Software Lead Jon McCormack Has Retired

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired.
  • Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October.
  • Revision 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

Revision 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.

McCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

He was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

Sources indicate that “Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack said. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

“My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

It’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the manufacturer than he was.
